introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Further Mathematics Paper 3 (0775), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2021. Duration: two and a half hours.**

Answer ALL questions. For your guidance, the approximate mark allocation for parts of each question is indicated in brackets. Mathematical formulae and tables, published by the Board, and noiseless non-programmable electronic calculators are allowed. In calculations, you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage.
enonce_intro_markdown: A particle $P$ of mass $m$ moves under gravity in a medium which offers a resistance to motion of magnitude $mkv^2$, where $v$ is the speed and $k$ is a positive constant.

questions.enonce_markdown: Show that it is possible for $P$ to fall vertically with steady speed $U$ whose value is to be determined. *[4 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
When $P$ falls, gravity $mg$ acts downwards and the resistance $mkv^2$ acts upwards, so taking downwards as positive

$$m\frac{dv}{dt} = mg - mkv^2.$$

A steady speed means $\dfrac{dv}{dt} = 0$ (weight balanced by the resistance):

$$mg - mkU^2 = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; U^2 = \frac{g}{k}.$$

Since $g > 0$ and $k > 0$, this has the positive solution $U = \sqrt{\dfrac{g}{k}}$, so a steady fall is possible. (The speed tends to this value: for $v < U$ the acceleration $g - kv^2$ is positive, for $v > U$ it is negative.)

$$\boxed{U = \sqrt{\frac{g}{k}},\quad\text{that is } k = \frac{g}{U^2}}$$

questions.enonce_markdown: The particle is projected vertically upwards with speed $2U$. Show that the maximum height above the point of projection is $\dfrac{U^2}{2g}\ln 5$. *[4 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
Let $x$ be the height above the point of projection. On the way up, gravity and the resistance both act downwards, so

$$m v\frac{dv}{dx} = -mg - mkv^2 = -mg\left(1 + \frac{v^2}{U^2}\right) = -\frac{mg}{U^2}\left(U^2 + v^2\right),$$

using $k = \dfrac{g}{U^2}$. Separating the variables:

$$\frac{v\,dv}{U^2 + v^2} = -\frac{g}{U^2}\,dx.$$

The speed falls from $2U$ at $x = 0$ to $0$ at the maximum height $H$:

$$\int_{2U}^{0}\frac{v\,dv}{U^2 + v^2} = -\frac{g}{U^2}\int_0^H dx,$$

$$\Big[\tfrac12\ln(U^2 + v^2)\Big]_{2U}^{0} = \tfrac12\ln U^2 - \tfrac12\ln(5U^2) = -\tfrac12\ln 5 = -\frac{gH}{U^2}.$$

Therefore

$$H = \frac{U^2}{2g}\ln 5. \qquad \blacksquare$$

questions.enonce_markdown: Show also that the time taken to attain this height is $\dfrac{U}{g}\tan^{-1}(2)$. *[5 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
On the way up, with $k = \dfrac{g}{U^2}$,

$$\frac{dv}{dt} = -g - kv^2 = -\frac{g}{U^2}\left(U^2 + v^2\right).$$

Separating the variables and integrating from $v = 2U$ at $t = 0$ to $v = 0$ at $t = T$:

$$\int_{2U}^{0}\frac{dv}{U^2 + v^2} = -\frac{g}{U^2}\int_0^T dt.$$

$$\left[\frac1U\tan^{-1}\frac{v}{U}\right]_{2U}^{0} = \frac1U\left(0 - \tan^{-1}2\right) = -\frac{gT}{U^2}.$$

Hence

$$T = \frac{U^2}{g}\cdot\frac{1}{U}\tan^{-1}2 = \frac{U}{g}\tan^{-1}(2). \qquad \blacksquare$$

Numerically $\tan^{-1}2 \approx 1.107$ rad, so $T \approx 1.107\,\dfrac{U}{g}$.
